questions.question: Examine the historical context that shaped Ambedkar’s socio-political activism / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Experience marked by Brahmanical dominance, caste oppression, untouchability,
  • social exclusion, and unequal access to education and public life. Struggle for reform,
  • dignity and political, legal and social rights

questions.solution_html:

  • restrictions on/ denial of access to public places, denial of education, occupational
  • stigma, dehumanisation, humiliation, social boycott, exclusion form civic and
  • religious institutions.

questions.question: Discuss the ideological differences between Ambedkar and Gandhi regarding caste reform. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Ambedkar- rejection of caste and call for its annihilation- caste as structurally rooted
  • in Hindu social order. Gandhi- call for reform within in the Hindu society- emphasis
  • on moral transformation of the oppressor- caste as an evil that can be corrected.

  • workforce, expanding employment, and reducing dependence on traditional caste
  • occupations.

questions.question: Assess the extent to which independent India has realised the goals envisioned in 'Annihilation of Caste' / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate level question. Areas where Ambedkar’s goals were realised- every citizen is
  • equal in legal terms- constitutional protections, reservation, civil rights, anti-
  • discrimination laws. Areas left unaddressed- law in practice, role of caste in shaping
  • social life, political power, access to resources- violence.

questions.question: Evaluate the political consequences of Ambedkar’s resignation over the stalling of the Hindu Code Bill. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Resignation due to slow pace of social reform- unwillingness of dominant political
  • forces to confront patriarchy. Ambedkar's resignation exposed the limits of post-
  • independence reformism, stood as a proof of how strong the conservative forces were
  • in an independent India. Highlighted the commitment of Ambedkar towards women’s
  • rights, legal equality, and secular social reform.

questions.solution_html:

  • social efficiency through harnessing the maximum potential of an individual.
  • Ambedkar's nationalism- argued for social justice- without social justice nationalism
  • remained hollow and reproduced caste domination and class elites.

questions.solution_html:

  • religion, endogamy and social power in sustaining the system. Solution- legal rights,
  • social reform, education, political representation, moral transformation- equality
  • transformed to a structural goal rather than philosophical.

  • reservations, and democratic safeguards. But a constitution is as good as those
  • enacting it and following it. Problems with implementation- caste, patriarchy,
  • domination by majority and inequality are still realities.
